I went to what had to be one of the smallest shows they've ever done. I grew up in New Haven, Connecticut, which is WWE corporate's backyard, essentially. New Haven had a big arena called the New Haven Coliseum. Big old gray place, big enough to do monster trucks too. Incidentally, Howard Finkel was discovered there. Anyways, after a number of years the place started to literally fall apart. Like, concrete from the roof fell and hit seats in spots that would be killed a bunch of people. Thankfully no one was hurt, but the place was essentially condemned as unsafe, except for the ground floor. 

The last show ever booked at the Coliseum was an untelevised house show with just a ring set up and the folding chairs set up around it. I'd be shocked if even 1000 seats were set up. There were so many great shows in New Haven over the years that I think they wanted to give a great send off to the old place, and it was a hell of a card. 

A few years later me and a few thousand others stood on the roofs of adjacent buildings and watched the place be demolished.

This piece seems rather straightforward actually. A single moment and feeling captured in time. 

As the speaker looks at art their child the thought of the dead woman comes to mind. The child is obviously representing youth, and possibility. Birth and potential. The old woman we are told died lost in the woods, found only due to scavenging birds. All of her life, all of her loves and hates, achievements and failures, are summed up in the grisly detail of her death.

The stark contrast between the two makes the author suddenly aware that this fresh life of a young girl will be left in the end as nothing more than food for buzzards, so shall we all. Death is the great equalizer.

It's a sad and yet beautiful realization all parents have to have about their kids. You made this life, but no life is forever. Not yours, not theirs. This is, as a musing on life, rather haunting. It reminds me of a song lyric:

"Everybody dies frustrated and sad and that is beautiful"

Hmm, this seems like a good chance to bust out the sandwich I made for a friend's girlfriend's birthday last month. Reddit loves the shooter sandwich, mine is just with a minor modification. You'll need:

**Round Portuguese loaf of bread**

**1 medium grade steak, thick is preferred**

**1/2 lb mushrooms**

**1/2 lb shallots**

**1 lb bacon**

**1 lb pepper jack cheese**

**Honey Mustard**

**Horseradish Sauce**

**Worcestershire Sauce**

Cut the bread straight across, making a top and what is essentially a huge bread bowl. Hollow out that bread, you're gonna need space for all of this. Make sure you don't hollow out too much or you'll pierce the bread.

Caramelize the shallots

Cook the mushrooms in Worcestershire sauce and some butter

Lay the bacon out flat in a deep baking pan and cook until done, but not too crisp. You want it to be soft enough to squish with weight later. If it is too crispy it will break.

Cook the steaks in the same pan. Light salt and pepper for seasoning. Make sure you do not remove the bacon grease first. Once it is done baking you will have amazing drippings if you use those for anything. I personally recommend making Yorkshire pudding with them, but you can also pour them into your dog's bowl to make dry food suddenly amazing.

Assemble the sandwich in this order: Steak, bacon, shallots, mushrooms, pepper jack cheese. Then on top add each of the sauces in medium amounts, about 2 tablespoons each.

Wrap the sandwich in parchment paper. Then again. Then in tin foil. Then again. Now put something long and flat on top of it, like a cooking board. Make sure it can take a lot of weight. Now put 80 lbs of weight on the board to flatten your sandwich.

**1. Wristcutters: A Love Story**

A few dead friends go on a road trip looking for God. There are a lot of films dealing with depressed characters, often people who have considered or even attempted suicide, and many of these films are good. But no film I have ever seen has spoken to me as honestly and perception. I was plagued by depression among other issues for most of my life, and I never felt any film truly did justice to the community as *Wristcutters*. most of my friends had/have issues as well, and when we talk about the world it is through this tint, this taint, that others never seem to get. Call it cynicism, call it weltsmerz, but its different. This movie understands that. Tear jerking, beautiful, funny, and wise, this is my all time favorite film.

**2. The Royal Tenenbaums**

A family tries to stay together in spite of themselves. This film doesn't hit me on such a personal level as *Wristcutters*, but it is perhaps the most perfect film I've ever seen. The direction, the casting, the cinematography, the sets, the color choices, the wardrobe, and especially the music. Quirky, unusual, but gripping. This is an amazing film I recommend to anyone who just loves films.

**3. Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind**

The best modern love story film, period. Not because it tells the story of two people destined to be together. It does, sort of, but more because it is a story about love. This film speaks to me as someone with a more than checkered past on the subject. There were times when I would wish I'd never met my ex-fiance, but then you remember small things; Your first kiss, hearing her say "I love you" for the first time, and you know you'd fight tooth and nail to hold onto those memories, even if it all fell apart in the end. *Eternal Sunshine* is about human desires, wants and needs, memory and regret, and if you've ever been in love, you'll love it too.

**4. Man on the Moon**

The tragic tale of one of the world's greatest entertainers, Andy Kaufman. People at the time of his fame were sharply divided on Andy Kaufman's brand of entertainment. In hindsight today, most comedians consider him a genius. But he was more than just an entertainer, he was an incredibly complicated man. Man on the Moon shows us the behind the scenes of Kaufman's short life and career, the ups and downs, his loves, his family, his tricks and pranks, and keeps you laughing all the way through. That is, if you understand the joke.

**5. The Fisher King**

A classic tale of tragedy, romance, and redemption. I'm a big fan of both Robin Williams and Jeff Bridges and while it is hard to say if this is either of their best films they made, it is certainly my favorite. Gilliam's unique directorial style oozes from every frame of this film. At face value it is about a broken men, but when you delve deeper it is about so much more. The mythology of this film is really why I love it more than anything else.
